key_insight: Instead of applying RL to output tokens or lengthy textual rationales, Reinforced Attention Learning (RAL) applies policy-gradient optimization directly to a model's internal attention distributions, producing stronger and more stable improvements for multimodal perception and reasoning.
problem_solved: Multimodal LLMs gain little — and can even degrade — when post-trained with token-level RL using verbose rationales; RAL addresses this by optimizing the model's internal attention behavior so downstream perception and reasoning improve without relying on long text explanations.
method: Treat attention weights/distributions as the policy actions and apply a policy-gradient objective to maximize task-specific rewards (e.g., perception accuracy, reasoning score).
Sample or perturb attention patterns during rollouts, evaluate them with downstream rewards, and update the attention policy using RL signals rather than token-level gradients.
Stabilize learning with regularization (e.g., divergence/penalty to keep near pretrained attention priors) and lightweight constraints to preserve base-model competencies.
impact: RAL offers a more direct, sample-efficient way to tune multimodal models for perception and reasoning, reducing reliance on verbose rationales and lowering the risk of degrading pretrained capabilities — useful for practitioners tuning MLLMs for vision+language tasks.
visual_elements: Side-by-side diagram: token-level RL (long rationale text) vs. RAL (attention map adjustments) to show where optimization happens.
Pipeline flowchart: sample attention pattern → compute downstream reward → policy-gradient update → updated attention behavior.
Bar/line chart: performance comparison on representative multimodal tasks (baseline, token-RL, RAL) showing gains and stability.
Iconography: attention-head heatmap, reward/signal icon, and a shield/lock to indicate regularization/stability.
paper_authors: Bangzheng Li, Jianmo Ni, Chen Qu, Ian Miao, Liu Yang
